title: Zhuangzi
dateDisplay: c. 4th–3rd centuries BCE (received recension, 3rd century CE)
author: zhuangzi
attributionNote: The book is named for Zhuang Zhou (c. 369–286 BCE), a minor official of the state of Song. Scholarship distinguishes the seven 'inner' books, which may be close to his own writing, from the outer and miscellaneous books compiled by later followers; the thirty-three-book recension was fixed by Guo Xiang in the third century CE from a larger collection of fifty-two.
description: The Zhuangzi is the second classic of Daoist philosophy: thirty-three books of parables, dialogues and anecdotes in which cooks and cicadas, cripples and shamans, Confucius and Laozi argue about the usefulness of the useless, the transformation of things, the limits of language and the art of living without harm. The inner books develop the teaching of the Dao as an unnameable process; the outer and miscellaneous books extend it into politics, death, craft and the strange. Its humour and imaginative range made it a foundation of Chinese literature as well as of Daoist thought.
historicalContext: The text grew over several centuries in the Warring States and early imperial periods, and its layers are visible in style and doctrine. Guo Xiang's edition and commentary (c. 300 CE) displaced the earlier recensions and became the received text. James Legge translated it for the Sacred Books of the East in 1891, the first complete English rendering; his introduction weighs the authenticity of the books and the meaning of the Dao, and his notes identify the Chinese commentators he follows.
availabilityNote: Complete. All thirty-three books of Legge's translation are streamed from the Internet Sacred Text Archive at read time, one printed book per chapter: books I–XVII from volume 39 and books XVIII–XXXIII from volume 40. The two volumes' introductions and the appendixes printed after the text in volume 40 are not part of the work. The archive's index prints Book XXIX, 'The Robber Kih', as Book XXIV; the chapter label follows the book's own heading and position.
